title: Light affliction (2 Corinthians 4:16–18)
hookLine: outwardly wasting, inwardly renewed day by day

cards: Light. That's Paul's word for his troubles. Light.
This is the man whose list we read two days ago: beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, lowered from a city wall in a basket. Later in this very letter he'll write that list down.
And here, a few verses after the clay jars, he calls it all light affliction. A friend who said that about a year like that might get a worried phone call.
So either Paul is in denial, or he's weighing his troubles against something so heavy that they really do feel light.

teach.b: Here are the lines, in the King James words: "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Two people in one body.
The outward one is wearing out, and Paul doesn't hide it: knees, eyes, energy, the face in the mirror. The inward one is being made new, and not once. Day by day.
Then the weighing: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." Hear it as a balance scale.
On one side, the affliction: real, but light, and only for a moment.
On the other, glory: a weight, and eternal. Paul isn't saying the suffering is small. He's saying it's small next to what it sits beside.
Then the last line says where to look: "the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." Temporal means for a time.
The hospital bracelet, the bills, the gray hair: real, and all for a time.
Some readers hear a promise about the life to come; some also hear something happening now, a little each day, an inner life renewed while the outer one tires. Not a single dramatic rescue.
Just today, and then today again.

how: Some Christians read 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 at funerals, in hospitals and in seasons of aging or illness, as words about an inner life renewed while the body wears out, and about a hope beyond what is seen.

games.q: you're Paul, writing to Corinth. you've just admitted that your outward man is perishing. what do you write next?
o: so we give up, and wait for the end.
yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
so we must guard the body above all.
games.why: "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." he names the wearing out, and doesn't stop there.

practice: Notice your outward self first, whatever aches or is tired, and let it be tired without judging it.

Then turn inward and ask what would make the inner person a little newer today: not a whole new life, just one small thing, a short walk, a psalm read slowly, a call to someone who makes you laugh, an early night.
If you pray, you can ask God for today's renewal, just today's.

wordCard.voice: Light affliction. Paul's name for real suffering, weighed against an eternal weight of glory, while the inward self is renewed day by day.
